stories.title: Trump's media bans 'deprive the public', press freedom groups argue
stories.summary: Press freedom groups are suing the Trump administration over its efforts to block mainstream US news outlets from covering the White House, according to court filings. The affected news outlets sued, arguing the White House was illegally discriminating against them because of the content of their coverage. A federal judge later ordered the White House to restore the credentials of the impacted journalists while their lawsuit plays out. The reporters later said they were allowed back into the White House complex. The White House has, however, continued to selectively bar journalists, which news organisations in the US argue violates their press freedom protections.
stories.editorialText: Press freedom groups are suing the Trump administration over its efforts to block mainstream US news outlets from covering the White House, according to court filings. The six plaintiffs, which include scholars, advocates and journalists, argue media bans issued by the White House violate the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which protects the press and freedom of speech. Their lawsuit comes after CNN, Politico and MSNOW brought a separate legal challenge over the White House's attempts to revoke or restrict their press access. The Knight First Amendment Institute and Yale Law School's Media and Information Access Clinic filed the legal case on the plaintiffs' behalf. reserveStories.editorialText: Researchers at the U of A and the University of Michigan have reported the creation of a graphene-based energy harvester that uses ambient radiation to run ultra-low-power temperature sensors. This is the second sensor created by the team whose overall goal is development of autonomous sensor systems that draw power from multiple sources in the environment — solar, thermal, acoustic, kinetic, nonlinear and ambient radiation. The team previously reported successful development of graphene-based solar cells that can be used to power temperature sensors. The team has three requirements for these sensors: they must use locally harvested energy, they must have a long unattended service life (potentially decades) and they must be able to operate at nanowatt-scale power. All three requirements have been met in the latest sensor utilizing ambient radiation. reserveStories.editorialText: Storms battered northern Europe on Sunday, cutting power to more than 150,000 homes, forcing the cancellation of hundreds of flights and silencing phone networks. Winds of up to 84 miles (135 kilometers) an hour were recorded in Argyll and Bute in western Scotland, and fallen trees and power cables blocked roads and rail lines across the country. More than 82,000 homes in Britain, nearly 60,000 in France and at least 10,000 in Germany had power cuts inflicted by the passage of storms Boelo and Austen within 24 hours of each other, authorities in the countries said. Britain's Energy Networks Association indicated that more than 400,000 homes had lost power at some stage during the storms. Part of the pier at Brighton on the southern England coast, unused since a fire in 2003, blew away in Storm Austen on Friday. The powerful winds also battered northern France across the Channel as Europe battled its first big autumn storms of the year and experts warned of more extreme weather events because of global warming. reserveStories.title: This design software reimagines everyday objects as self-aware devices
reserveStories.summary: MIT researchers developed X-Hinges, software that helps design 3D-printed objects with built-in sensors. The tricky part is separating the sensors’ signals from interference caused by the wire-like connections around them. The tool places two different materials in the design to reduce that interference. The researchers describe objects such as lamps and gloves that respond to touch, as well as small robots and toys. It is an understandable electronics problem: make an object sense what someone is doing, then get a clear signal out of it.
reserveStories.editorialText: As a child, you likely saw a few Disney movies depicting inanimate objects, such as clocks, cups, and toys, as interactive companions to humans — an act of pure magic, seemingly. But scientists at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) are now doing something similar: transforming stationary items into self-aware tools that perceive and respond to human motion to complete a task. Engineers have 3D-printed these dynamic items with built-in sensing, using conductive materials for sensors and traces (sort of like wires) inside. The issue: both components were typically fabricated using the same material, so they’d emit similar signals. reserveStories.title: Demand for UK government action 10 months after British man’s death in Grenada
reserveStories.summary: A time-critical investigation into the death of a British father whose body was found in a ransacked property on the Caribbean island of Grenada has stalled because of diplomatic delays between the two countries. Charity workers supporting the family of Andrew Frederick are demanding immediate government intervention to clear the path for a full investigation to begin almost 10 months after his death, which has been ruled a homicide by a pathologist. The Murdered Abroad charity has called on the foreign affairs select committee to step in after Grenadian police found there was “no basis … that any homicide has occurred” and closed the case.

reserveStories.summary: More than one million supporters of Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, have streamed on to Rio’s most famous beach for a giant protest they hope will propel him towards a historic election fightback against his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro. Nearly 159m Brazilians will vote in the election’s runoff on Sunday, with the pair tied in the polls after Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October by 47% to 45%. Never since the return of democracy to Brazil in the 1980s has the first-round loser managed to bounce back.

Nearly 159m Brazilians will vote in the election’s runoff on Sunday, with the pair tied in the polls after Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October by 47% to 45%. On Saturday, under a fierce sun, red-clad crowds packed the 2.5-mile Copacabana beach in an attempt to help Lula clinch a dramatic and unprecedented comeback. Never since the return of democracy to Brazil in the 1980s has the first-round loser managed to bounce back.
reserveStories.imageCaption: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was cheered by a huge crowd on Copacabana beach on Saturday amid hopes he can secure an historic fourth term. Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/Reuters
